title: [Draft ML] The Clever Little Rabbit and the Proud Lion
summary: [Draft ML] When a mighty lion terrifies the forest animals, a tiny but clever rabbit uses wisdom and a deep jungle well to restore peace.
full_text:
[Draft ML] Deep in the whispering forest of Chandravan lived a mighty lion named Bhasuraka. He was strong, fierce, and proud. Every single morning, he roared so loudly that the trees trembled, hunting far more animals than he ever needed for his meal. The birds grew silent, the deer hid behind thickets, and the woodland was filled with worry.

One afternoon, the wise elders of the forest—the grandmother elephant, the spotted deer, and the little brown rabbit—gathered by the riverbank. 'If Bhasuraka continues like this,' said the deer, 'soon none of us will remain.' They decided to speak gently with the lion. The elders walked to the lion's den and bowed politely. 'O King of the Forest,' spoke the elephant, 'hunting every creature wastes the forest's life. We promise to send one animal peacefully each day to your door, so you need not tire yourself, and our families may live without terror.' The proud lion agreed, with one stern warning: 'If anyone is late by a single heartbeat, I will consume the entire woodland.'

Many peaceful days passed until it was the turn of a tiny rabbit named Chatura. Chatura was small, with soft velvety ears and bright inquisitive eyes. His companions wept as they bade him farewell, but Chatura smiled warmly. 'Do not weep, dear friends,' he whispered. 'Physical strength is grand, but a calm mind can solve what muscles cannot.'

Chatura deliberately took his time. He rested beneath shady banyan leaves, munched sweet clovers, watched the gentle clouds drift by, and listened to the bubbling creek. By the time the sunset painted the sky in shades of amber and violet, the lion was furious. His stomach was growling like thunder.

When Chatura finally hopped toward the den, Bhasuraka sprang up, teeth bared. 'You puny speck of fluff!' roared the lion. 'How dare you keep me waiting? I shall gobble you up and destroy all your friends before sunrise!'

Chatura bowed with complete tranquility. 'Majesty,' he said in a calm, respectful tone, 'it is not my fault. Three other rabbits and I set out at noon to serve you. But on the way, another enormous lion stepped out from an ancient stone fortress. He roared that he is the true king of this forest. He captured my companions and sent me only to warn you.'

Bhasuraka's pride flared like wild flames. 'Another lion in my kingdom? Take me to him at once!'

Chatura hopped ahead, leading the furious lion to an ancient, deep stone well near the forest edge. The water inside was crystal-clear and calm as a mirror. 'He is hiding down inside his fortress, Your Majesty,' said the rabbit, pointing with his ear.

Bhasuraka peered over the stone wall. Looking straight back up at him was the face of a fierce lion with blazing eyes. When Bhasuraka opened his jaws and unleashed a deafening roar, the deep well echoed the roar back at twice the volume. Seeing his reflection mimic his rage and hearing the roaring echo, Bhasuraka believed his rival was defying him. Without a second thought, he leapt down into the well to battle the illusion.

The forest instantly fell quiet. Chatura smiled, thanked the cool water, and hopped joyfully back to his family. From that day forward, the animals of Chandravan lived in harmony and safety, always remembering that true wisdom is greater than raw force.

full_text:
[Draft ML] One crisp autumn morning, Emperor Akbar and his favourite minister, Birbal, were strolling through the royal palace gardens. Dewdrops sparkled like diamonds on jasmine petals, and flock after flock of sleek black crows fluttered among the leafy mango trees, cawing cheerfully to one another.

Akbar paused and watched a crow land gracefully upon a marble fountain. A mischievous thought blossomed in the Emperor's mind. He loved testing the sharp wit of his courtiers, especially Birbal.

Turning with a serious expression, Akbar asked, 'Tell me, Birbal, you are famous for knowing the answer to every riddle under the sun. Can you tell me exactly how many crows reside in our entire imperial city?'

Birbal looked at the crows. He closed his eyes for a quiet moment, as though mentally counting every rooftop, garden branch, and riverbank across the empire. The other courtiers nearby smirked, believing that this time, Birbal was finally trapped by an impossible question.

Birbal opened his eyes, smiled with genuine warmth, and bowed gracefully. 'Your Imperial Majesty, there are exactly ninety-five thousand, four hundred and sixty-three crows in our city.'

Akbar raised his eyebrow, thoroughly astonished. 'Are you certain of this exact count, Birbal? What if our royal guards conduct a census and find there are more crows than you stated?'

Birbal chuckled softly. 'If there are more, Huzoor, it simply means that relatives from neighbouring kingdoms have flown in to visit their families for the holidays.'

Akbar suppressed a smile, eager to test him further. 'And what if my guards count fewer crows than your number?'

'Then, Majesty,' Birbal answered without a heartbeat of hesitation, 'it only proves that some of our city's crows have flown away on vacation to visit their dear relatives in faraway lands.'

Emperor Akbar burst into hearty laughter that echoed across the fragrant gardens. He admired Birbal not just for his quick intelligence, but because his humor was always joyful, kind, and harm-free. Akbar removed a string of pearls from his cloak and gifted it to Birbal with great admiration.

full_text:
[Draft ML] On the sunlit hills of Thessaly, Swift the Hare was known as the fastest animal in the valley. His hind legs were like coiled springs, and he could dash across clover meadows in the blink of an eye. Unfortunately, Swift was also terribly boastful. He spent hours teasing the gentle creatures who walked at a calm pace.

'Look at you, Plod the Tortoise!' laughed Swift one morning, kicking up a cloud of dust. 'You carry your house on your back and take all day just to reach the foot of the hill. I could run to the top and back three times before you take ten steps!'

Plod poked his wrinkly head from his shell and smiled with patient goodwill. 'You run like the autumn breeze, Swift,' said Plod gently. 'Yet haste often trips on its own heels. Would you care to race to the great oak tree at the valley's crest?'

The Hare roared with laughter. 'A race against a tortoise? This will be the funniest spectacle the valley has ever seen!'

The wise old Fox agreed to mark the course and act as the honest judge. At sunrise, animals from all around gathered along the green path. The squirrels chattered, the badgers clapped, and the bluebirds sang from branch to branch.

'Ready... Steady... Go!' barked the Fox.

Swift shot forward like an arrow released from a bow. Within seconds, he was far ahead, a tiny dot dashing over the rolling slopes. Plod, meanwhile, placed one green foot forward, then the next. Step by step, slow and rhythmic, he began his journey under the warm morning sun.

Halfway up the long hill, Swift looked over his shoulder. The tortoise was barely visible near the starting line. 'I have plenty of time,' thought Swift with a chuckle. 'The sun is warm, the wild lavender smells sweet, and a quick nap will be delightful. Even if Plod walks all morning, I can overtake him in five leaps.'

Swift curled up beneath a shady willow tree and drifted off into a deep, peaceful sleep.

Meanwhile, the sun climbed higher in the sky. Plod never stopped. He did not rush, nor did he halt to gaze at the butterflies. He kept his eyes on the winding trail ahead, breathing evenly, taking one steady step after another. Hours slipped quietly past.

When Swift finally opened his eyes, the afternoon light was turning golden. He stretched his paws, yawned, and glanced casually back down the path. To his shock, the path behind was empty! He whipped his head toward the finish line—and there, just a single step away from the great oak tree, was Plod, greeted by the cheering applause of all the woodland friends.

Swift sprinted with all his might, kicking up dust like a whirlwind, but it was too late. Plod gently touched the oak bark with his front foot.

The Hare hung his long ears in humility. Plod offered his paw with warm sportsmanship. 'Never mock someone who moves at their own pace, friend,' said Plod. 'Slow and steady wins the race.'
moral: [Draft ML] Consistent patience and steady effort accomplish far more than careless haste.

title: [Draft ML] The Empty Flowerpot and the Honest Child
summary: [Draft ML] An aging emperor gives every child in the province a flower seed to test their character. Only young Ling possesses the courage of pure honesty.
full_text:
[Draft ML] Long ago, in a peaceful province framed by misty bamboo mountains, lived an elderly ruler named Emperor Han. The Emperor was beloved by his people for his fairness, but he had no children to inherit the responsibility of caring for the land. As the autumn of his life drew near, he pondered deeply on how to choose the next custodian of the realm.

'A leader must possess sharp wisdom, but above all, an unyielding heart of honesty,' the Emperor said to his counsellors.

The next day, a proclamation was sounded through every village. All the children of the land were invited to the palace gates. Each child was handed a small clay bowl and a single black seed. 'Take this seed home,' announced the Emperor with a gentle smile. 'Plant it in the richest soil, water it with devotion, and bring it back to me exactly one year from today. The child who grows the truest flower shall be chosen as my successor.'

Among the children was a quiet boy named Ling. Ling loved plants dearly. In his little garden behind his grandmother's cottage, sweet orchids and vibrant honeysuckles blossomed under his tender care. Ling carefully placed the seed in an earthen pot, adding compost, rich loam, and fresh spring water.

Days turned into weeks. Ling tended the pot every morning and evening. He placed it where the morning sun was sweetest and shielded it from cold midnight winds. Yet, weeks passed, and not a single green sprout pushed through the dark soil.

Ling transferred the seed into a larger glazed pot with richer earth, but still, nothing grew. Meanwhile, his classmates in the village boasted loudly. 'Look at my splendid jade lily!' cheered one. 'My peony is growing tall and fragrant!' bragged another.

Ling felt a heavy knot in his stomach. 'Grandmother, why will my seed not grow? Did I do something wrong?'

His wise grandmother placed her hand over his. 'You gave it pure water, rich soil, and honest care, Ling. You have done your best. Whatever happens, bring your honest effort before the Emperor.'

A full year passed, and the children gathered at the palace square. The courtyard looked like a magnificent ocean of radiant blossoms—scarlet roses, golden chrysanthemums, and towering blue bells. Every child held a dazzling flowerpot, proud and eager.

Ling stood in the back row, holding his plain earthen pot filled only with dark, empty earth. Several children whispered and giggled at him, but Ling stood straight, holding his pot with quiet dignity.

Emperor Han walked slowly through the ranks of children. He inspected the blossoms, but his face remained solemn. He did not smile at the towering roses, nor did he praise the fragrant orchids. When he reached the end of the courtyard, his gaze fell upon Ling and his barren pot.

'Child,' asked the Emperor gently, 'why is your pot empty? Did you not plant the seed I gave you?'

Ling bowed respectfully, tears glistening in his eyes. 'Your Majesty, I planted your seed in fertile soil. I watered it every day and protected it from storms. But it simply would not grow. I am sorry, Sire. This empty pot is the only truth I have to offer.'

A luminous smile spread across the Emperor's face. He took Ling by the hand, turned toward the gathering, and spoke in a clear, ringing voice:

'People of the realm, behold your next leader! Before I gave out the seeds a year ago, I had every single one boiled so that none could ever sprout. All these magnificent flowers grew from different seeds brought in when my seed failed. Only this child had the courage to bring an empty pot. Ling gave me the rarest blossom of all—the flower of pure honesty.'
moral: [Draft ML] Honesty requires profound courage, and true integrity is more valuable than counterfeit success.

title: [Draft ML] The Little Hummingbird and the Forest Fire

full_text:
[Draft ML] High above the emerald valleys of the Andes, the ancient forest whispered with life. Bromeliads cling to mossy cedar branches, spectacled bears foraged for wild berries, and bright toucans sang among the clouds. Among them lived Colibrí, a tiny hummingbird whose feathers shimmered with shades of ruby, gold, and sapphire.

One dry summer afternoon, a sharp bolt of dry lightning touched an old pine tree. Soon, thin ribbons of smoke wound into the air, and crackling flames began to leap through the dry brush. The animals panicked. The mighty jaguar leaped across the creek to flee, the tapirs stampeded toward the open plains, and the monkeys swung hurriedly away into the distance.

Everyone fled—except little Colibrí.

She zipped down to the mountain stream, dipped her slender beak into the cool water, and held a single shimmering droplet. Flying swiftly toward the smoke, she dropped that tiny bead of water upon the advancing flames. Then she zipped back to the stream, gathered another drop, and released it again. Back and forth she flew, her wings whirring at eighty beats per second, a flash of brave iridescent light amidst the rising smoke.

Watching from the safety of the distant riverbank, the armadillo shook his head. 'Colibrí!' he shouted. 'What foolishness is this? You are smaller than a leaf! Your tiny drops of water cannot possibly put out a giant forest fire! Save yourself!'

Colibrí paused for half a second in mid-air, her dark eyes shining with determination. 'I know my drops are small, friend,' she sang back. 'I know I cannot extinguish this fire alone. But this forest is our home. I am doing my part.'

With that, she dove back into the river for another drop.

The animals on the riverbank fell completely silent. The mighty jaguar looked down at his powerful paws. The tapirs looked at their broad backs. The mountain condor spread his immense wings. 'If a creature as fragile as Colibrí will not abandon our home,' rumbled the jaguar, 'how can we, who have great strength, stand here doing nothing?'

The condor soared high and beat his giant wings to blow the smoke away. The tapirs and bears scooped water into large gourds and threw it across the dry grass. The elephants of the lowlands sprayed gallons of river water through their trunks. The monkeys passed damp moss from branch to branch.

Working together, drop by drop, gourd by gourd, the animals smothered the sparks and cooled the embers. By sunset, a gentle drizzle fell from the clearing sky, washing away the ash.

The animals gathered around the little hummingbird, who was resting on a soft fern leaf, her feathers glowing in the twilight. They realized that greatness is not measured by the size of one's wings, but by the size of one's caring heart.

[Draft ML] Once upon a time, in a peaceful valley framed by rolling meadows, lived a sweet-natured girl named Ella. Ella had eyes that sparkled with curiosity and a voice as gentle as morning rain. After her dear mother and father passed away, Ella lived with her cold-hearted stepmother and two vain stepsisters. They made Ella sleep in the chilly attic and dress in patched smocks. Because she worked near the fireplace and sat by the hearth to keep warm, they mockingly called her 'Cinderella.'

Yet, despite the rough scrubbing, sweeping, and mending, Ella never let bitterness harden her spirit. She sang softly to the sparrows perched on the windowsill, shared crumbs with the tiny mice who lived beneath the floorboards, and planted sweet-smelling lavender in the garden. She believed deeply in what her mother had once whispered to her: 'Have courage, and be kind, for kindness is a magic that never fades.'

One winter evening, trumpets sounded throughout the kingdom. The King was hosting a grand starlight celebration at the royal palace, and every young person in the realm was invited. Cinderella's stepsisters squealed with excitement, demanding silk dresses, silver ribbons, and powdered wigs. Ella worked day and night ironing their ruffles and polishing their buckles. When they departed in their fine coach, Cinderella sat down by the kitchen embers and wept softly into her apron.

'Why do you weep, sweet child?' asked a voice as gentle as starlight.

Ella looked up in wonder. Standing before her was an elderly woman with silver hair, carrying a slender wand that glowed with warm golden sparks. It was her benevolent fairy guardian.

'I wish with all my heart that I could visit the palace ballroom just once,' whispered Ella.

'Because you have guarded a pure and generous heart, your wish shall be granted,' smiled the guardian. 'Run to the garden and fetch the plumpest pumpkin, and bring the little mice from the pantry.'

With a gentle wave of the wand, the orange pumpkin swelled into a majestic golden carriage with velvet cushions. The six friendly garden mice transformed into sleek dapple-gray horses with braided manes. A gentle grasshopper became a proud coachman. Finally, the fairy touched Ella's faded gown. In a swirl of shimmering light, her patched apron turned into a magnificent gown of starlit azure silk, embroidered with silver threads. On her feet appeared a pair of delicate, luminous slippers made of pure spun glass.

'Go and enjoy the dance, Ella,' cautioned the guardian with a loving smile. 'But remember this one solemn truth: the spell holds only until the twelfth stroke of midnight. If you linger a moment longer, your carriage will become a pumpkin again, and your gown will return to hearth-cloth.'

When Cinderella arrived at the palace ballroom, the room fell breathless. The Prince was captivated not merely by her radiant appearance, but by her gentle manners, her thoughtful conversation, and the sincere warmth she showed to the palace musicians and servants. They danced together like two leaves floating upon a calm stream.

Suddenly, the great palace clock began to chime midnight: *Dong... Dong... Dong...*

Remembering her promise, Cinderella curtsied swiftly and ran down the grand marble staircase. In her haste, one of her delicate glass slippers slipped from her foot and remained behind upon the steps. By the time she reached the courtyard gates, the twelfth chime struck. The golden coach vanished, the horses scampered away into the grass as mice, and Ella found herself in her worn smock once more, walking home under the quiet stars—holding only the single glass slipper in her pocket.

The next day, royal heralds announced that the Prince would search the entire realm to find the owner of the glass slipper, for he knew that the true beauty of that young lady was rooted in her grace and honesty. The heralds visited every grand villa and manor. When they reached Cinderella's cottage, the stepmother and sisters tried desperately to force their feet into the tiny glass slipper, but it would not fit.

'Is there no other maiden in this house?' inquired the royal envoy.

'Only a ragged kitchen girl,' scoffed the stepmother.

The envoy smiled kindly and asked Ella to step forward. She sat calmly upon the wooden bench, and the envoy placed the slipper near her foot. It slipped on effortlessly, fitting perfectly like a second skin. From her apron pocket, Ella gently drew the matching slipper.

The stepsisters fell to their knees in astonishment and pleaded for forgiveness. Ella took them by the hands, smiled with heartfelt sincerity, and forgave them completely. Cinderella was welcomed to the royal palace, where she and the Prince dedicated their lives to helping the needy, fostering peace, and teaching all people that true nobility comes from kindness, humility, and love.

[Draft ML] On the lush banks of the holy river Ganga stood a grand rose-apple tree with dense emerald leaves and bunches of ruby-red, honey-sweet fruit. In this tree lived Raktamukha, a cheerful and generous monkey. Every day, he swung gracefully from branch to branch, enjoying the sweet fruit and the river breeze.

One afternoon, an exhausted crocodile named Karalamukha crawled out of the rushing river onto the sandy bank. Seeing that the reptile was weak from hunger, the kind monkey plucked a handful of ripe, juicy rose-apples and tossed them down. The crocodile ate them gratefully. They were the sweetest morsels he had ever tasted.

From that day onward, Karalamukha visited the tree every afternoon. The monkey and the crocodile spent long, peaceful hours discussing the ways of the forest and the river. The monkey always showered his friend with the finest fruit, and the crocodile carried some home across the river to share with his wife.

However, the crocodile's wife was greedy and cold-hearted. One day she hissed, 'If this monkey feeds on these divine sweet rose-apples day and night, think how sweet his heart must be! Bring me his heart to eat, or I shall leave this river forever.'

Karalamukha was troubled. He did not wish to betray his dearest friend, but under his wife's nagging pressure, he gave in. Swimming back across the river, he invited the monkey to his home. 'Friend monkey, my wife has prepared a banquet of river delicacies to thank you for all your kindness. Hop upon my back, and I shall carry you across the river.'

Raktamukha, suspecting nothing evil in a friend, gladly leapt onto the crocodile's broad, scaly back. Karalamukha swam into the middle of the deep river. Once they reached the deepest waters where the monkey could not jump ashore, the crocodile began to sink into the waves.

'Friend! Why are you swimming so deep?' cried the monkey, spitting water. 'I cannot swim!'

The crocodile sighed with guilt. 'Forgive me, monkey. My wife demands your heart to eat, and I am taking you to her.'

The monkey's heart skipped a beat, but he did not scream or panic. He took a deep breath, gathered his wits, and spoke with calm laughter:

'My dear friend, why did you not tell me this before we set out? I would gladly offer my heart for your household's happiness! But we monkeys keep our hearts safely stored on the highest branches of our rose-apple tree to prevent them from getting bruised when we leap between trees! I left my heart behind on the branch today.'

The foolish crocodile believed him. 'Is that so? Then we must turn around immediately!'

Karalamukha swung his heavy tail and swam swiftly back to the bank. The moment they reached the shallows, the monkey leapt like an arrow off the crocodile's back, scrambled up the trunk, and perched safely on the highest bough of the rose-apple tree.

'Come down with your heart, friend!' called the crocodile from below.

Raktamukha laughed with pity and wisdom. 'You foolish reptile! Can any living creature exist with its heart outside its body? You betrayed a friend who fed you when you were starving. Go back to your river. True friendship cannot live where trust has died.'

The crocodile hung his snout in shame and swam away into the deep mud, while the monkey continued to live safely in the high branches, forever grateful for his calm presence of mind.

The streams had dried into cracked mud, and the village animal troughs were bone-dry. Corvus felt his throat parched and his wings heavy with fatigue.

Just as he was about to lose hope, his sharp black eyes spotted an earthen pitcher resting on the stone patio of an abandoned farmhouse garden. Corvus fluttered down and landed eagerly upon the rim of the jug.

He peered inside. To his delight, there was clear, sparkling water at the bottom! But his joy turned to dismay when he stretched his neck downward. The pitcher was tall with a narrow neck, and the water level was low. No matter how much Corvus stretched, his beak stopped two inches short of the water's surface.

He tried to push the heavy clay jar over with his wings, hoping to spill the water onto the flat stones. But the pitcher was made of thick terracotta and filled with too much weight; it stood firm and would not budge. If he knocked it too hard and broke it, the precious water would vanish into the dry soil before he could take a single sip.

Corvus rested on a stone wall, panting. A weaker bird might have given up in despair. But Corvus paused, looked around the garden patio, and used his brilliant mind.

His eyes fell upon a pile of smooth, round pebbles scattered along the gravel path. A spark of scientific inspiration ignited in his bird brain!

Corvus hopped over to the gravel path, picked up a small round pebble in his beak, flew back to the pitcher, and dropped it inside: *Plink!*

He picked up a second pebble and dropped it in: *Plop!*

A third pebble: *Plunk!*

At first, the water level seemed barely to move. It was slow, tedious, and tiring work. But Corvus did not lose heart. He flew back and forth with steady rhythm: pebble by pebble, stone by stone. One, five, ten, twenty, forty pebbles sank to the bottom of the pitcher. With each stone that entered, the water had no choice but to rise higher through displacement.

The North Wind puffed his icy cheeks and roared with thunderous pride: 'I am the mightiest force in all nature! The Sun smiled with gentle, calm warmth. 'Strength, dear brother Wind, is not measured only by how loudly you howl or how much destruction you cause. True power lies in gentle persuasion and warmth.'

The North Wind scoffed in disbelief. 'Persuasion? Softness is weakness! Let us have a contest to settle this once and for all.'

Looking down at the earth, the Sun spotted a solitary traveler walking along a winding mountain path. The traveler was wrapped tightly in a thick woolen cloak to protect himself from the autumn chill.

'Look at that traveler,' proposed the Sun. 'Whichever of us can cause that traveler to take off his woolen cloak shall be recognized as the more powerful.'

'A child's play!' boomed the North Wind. 'I shall blow his cloak clean off his shoulders in three seconds. Stand aside and watch!'

The Sun stepped behind a fluffy silver cloud, giving the North Wind first turn.

The North Wind took a tremendous, freezing breath and blew with all his fury: *WHOOOOOSH!* Gusts of icy gale swept down the mountain. Hail and dried leaves spun in violent whirlwinds. The traveler staggered, nearly losing his footing on the rocky ledge.

Did the traveler let go of his cloak? Far from it! The harder and colder the North Wind blew, the tighter the traveler clutched the woolen fabric against his chest, wrapping the edges around his neck and buttoning every clasp securely against the storm!

The North Wind roared in frustration, howling until his lungs were completely exhausted. After fifteen minutes of raging fury, the wind died down to a tired whimper. The traveler remained completely cloaked, shivering but unyielding.

Now it was the Sun's turn.

The Sun emerged gracefully from behind the cloud. He did not roar, demand, or use violence. He simply shone with radiant, steady, affectionate warmth. His golden rays bathed the hillside, the autumn wildflowers, and the winding path in comforting golden light.

Soon, the biting chill evaporated. The birds began singing in the olive groves. The traveler stopped shivering and unclasped the top button of his collar. As the Sun shone a little warmer and brighter, the traveler felt the soothing heat upon his shoulders and back. He wiped a bead of sweat from his forehead.

Finally, feeling wonderfully warm and comfortable, the traveler unbuttoned the cloak, slipped it off his shoulders with a sigh of relief, folded it neatly, and laid it over his arm as he walked merrily forward under the friendly sunshine.

The North Wind hung his head in silent astonishment. The Sun smiled kindly upon his brother: 'You see, dear Wind? Gentleness, warmth, and kind persuasion can accomplish what fury and force can never achieve.'

[Draft ML] Once upon a time, a hardworking donkey had carried sacks of grain to the mill for many long years. But as his strength waned with old age, his ungrateful master planned to sell him away. Sensation of danger in the air, the clever donkey decided to make his own way in the world. 'I will go to the free city of Bremen,' he thought cheerfully, 'and become a town musician!'

As he trotted along the highway, he found an old hunting hound lying by the roadside, panting wearily. 'Why are you sighing so, old fellow?' asked the donkey.

'Ah,' sighed the hound, 'because I am old and can no longer sprint through the brush to catch foxes, my master wanted to get rid of me. So I ran away, but how shall I earn my bread?'

'Come with me to Bremen!' brayed the donkey warmly. 'I shall play the lute, and you can beat the drums. Together, we shall make grand music!' The hound wagged his tail happily and joined him.

A little further down the road, they met an old ginger cat sitting with a face as gloomy as three rainy days. 'What ails you, whiskered friend?' asked the donkey.

'Now that I am getting gray, my teeth are worn down, and I prefer sitting by the stove purring instead of chasing mice, my mistress wanted to drown me!' wept the cat. 'Where shall I go?'

'You understand night serenades!' said the donkey. 'Join our band and come to Bremen!' The cat beamed and trotted beside them.

Soon, they passed a farmyard where a red rooster was crowing with all his might atop the gate: *Cock-a-doodle-doo!*

'Why are you screeching so loudly?' asked the donkey.

'Guests are coming for Sunday dinner, and the cook plans to put me in the soup pot tonight!' cried the rooster. 'So I am crowing while I still have my throat!'

'Red-comb,' laughed the donkey, 'come with us! Anything is better than the soup pot! You have a magnificent voice; together our quartet will astonish the world!'

By nightfall, the four friends were deep in a dark, whispering forest, still far from Bremen. The donkey and hound curled beneath a large beech tree, while the cat climbed the lower branches, and the rooster flew to the very top.

From the treetop, the rooster called down: 'Friends, I see a cozy warm light glowing through the trees not far away!'

They walked toward the light and discovered a sturdy cottage hidden in the woods. Peering through the illuminated window, the tall donkey saw a table laden with hot roasted potatoes, savory pies, and cider—and around it sat a band of rough robbers celebrating their spoils!

The four friends put their heads together and devised a brilliant plan to drive the robbers away.

The donkey placed his front hooves upon the windowsill. The hound leapt upon the donkey's back. The cat scrambled atop the hound's shoulders. And the rooster flew up and perched proudly upon the cat's head!

At a signal from the donkey, they began their grand symphony together with all their might! The donkey brayed: *HEE-HAW!* The hound barked: *WOOF-WOOF!* The cat meowed: *MEEE-OWWW!* And the rooster screeched: *COCK-A-DOODLE-DOO!* Then they plunged through the windowpane with a tremendous crash of glass!

The terrified robbers leapt from their seats, convinced that a four-headed forest monster had burst through the wall! Screaming in sheer panic, the bandits fled into the pitch-black forest and never dared return.

The four friends laughed with boundless joy. They sat down at the table and feasted upon the delicious pies until their bellies were round. Then they blew out the candles: the donkey slept in the warm straw, the dog behind the door, the cat by the warm hearth, and the rooster atop the roof beam.

They loved their cozy woodland home so dearly that they never needed to journey to Bremen after all, living together in peace, music, and lasting friendship for the rest of their happy days.

title: [Draft ML] The Emperor's New Clothes
summary: [Draft ML] Two cunning swindlers weave invisible clothes for a vain Emperor, claiming the cloth cannot be seen by anyone unfit for their post. Only an innocent child has the courage to speak the truth.

full_text:
[Draft ML] Many years ago, in a grand European capital, lived an Emperor who loved luxurious clothes more than anything else in the world. He did not care for his army, nor for the theatre, nor for caring for the poor; he cared only for parading in magnificent new garments. He had a different coat for every hour of the day.

One day, two cunning swindlers arrived in the city, posing as master weavers from a distant land. They claimed they could weave the most exquisite fabric ever beheld—a cloth whose colors and patterns were of peerless beauty. But its most miraculous quality, they declared, was that the fabric was completely invisible to anyone who was either hopelessly incompetent at their job or utterly stupid!

'Magnificent!' thought the vain Emperor. 'If I wore clothes made of such fabric, I could instantly discover which ministers in my government are unfit for their offices, and I could tell the wise from the foolish! I must have this cloth woven at once!'

The Emperor gave the swindlers large sums of gold and baskets of pure silk and gold thread. The weavers set up two large looms in a royal chamber and pretended to work furiously day and night. But in truth, there was not a single thread upon the empty looms, and they tucked all the gold and silk safely inside their knapsacks!

After a week, the Emperor sent his oldest, most trusted minister to check on the weavers' progress. The old minister entered the room and looked at the looms. His eyes widened in panic: *'Heaven forbid! I cannot see a single thread!'*

'Look at this delicate azure weave!' said one swindler, pointing at the empty air. 'Do you not admire the radiant pattern, Lord Minister?'

The poor minister broke into a cold sweat. *'Am I stupid?'* he thought in dread. *'Am I unfit for my high office? I dare not let anyone know that I see nothing!'* So he nodded enthusiastically: 'Oh, it is breathtaking! The colors! The intricate gold embroidery! I shall tell His Majesty immediately!'

Every courtier and general sent by the Emperor did the exact same thing. No one wanted to appear foolish or incompetent, so everyone praised the invisible cloth to the skies: 'Superb! Magnificent!'

Finally, the grand day arrived. The swindlers held up their empty hands, pretending to drape the Emperor in trousers, coat, and a long royal train. 'Behold, Sire! The garment is as light as a spider's web; you will feel as if you are wearing nothing at all!'

The Emperor posed before his tall mirror, turning this way and that in his underwear, pretending to admire the drape. 'How well it fits! How elegantly it hangs!' he exclaimed nervously, terrified of admitting he was stark naked.

The Emperor marched out into the public square beneath a grand velvet canopy to lead the royal procession. Thousands of citizens lined the streets, waving flags. Everyone had heard of the magic fabric, and no one wanted their neighbors to think they were stupid, so the whole crowd cheered: 'Oh! Look at the Emperor's new clothes! How marvelous! How divine!'

Then, from the front row of the crowd, perched upon her father's shoulders, a little girl tilted her head in confusion. Pointing with her tiny finger, she called out in a clear, sweet voice that echoed over the cheering:

*'But he isn't wearing anything at all!'*

A stunned silence fell over the square. The father blushed and whispered, 'Listen to the innocent child!' Then one neighbor whispered to another: 'The child says he has no clothes on!'

'He has no clothes on!' whispered someone else. And suddenly, the whole crowd of thousands of people erupted into a roar of laughter: *'He isn't wearing anything at all!'*

The Emperor shivered. He realized in his burning heart that the child was speaking the honest truth! But he was too proud to stop. So he held his head higher than ever, and his noble chamberlains walked behind him, diligently carrying a royal train that did not exist at all, while the honest truth echoed freely through the sunny streets.

title: [Draft ML] The Secret of the King's Royal Brinjals

full_text:
[Draft ML] In the royal botanical garden of Vijayanagara, King Krishna Deva Raya cultivated a rare variety of brinjal (eggplant). The vegetables were deep violet, extraordinarily sweet, and guarded day and night by armed royal sentries. No citizen was permitted to pick or taste even a single leaf under penalty of severe punishment.

One evening, the King hosted a small dinner for his closest ministers and served a curry prepared from the royal brinjals. Tenali Rama was enchanted by its rich, succulent flavor. When he returned home, he spoke so poetically about the delicious dish that his wife, Sharada, longed to prepare it for their young son, little Ramu.

'Can you not bring just two brinjals from the royal garden?' pleaded Sharada. 'Our child has never tasted such a delicacy.'

Tenali hesitated. Stealing royal produce was treason, but seeing his wife's pleading eyes, he made up his mind to pluck two brinjals under moonlight. Scaling the palace garden wall with agile footwork, he plucked two ripe brinjals and slipped home unnoticed. Sharada cooked a fragrant, mouthwatering curry and fed it to little Ramu, who ate with round-eyed joy.

However, Tenali realized a serious danger: Ramu was only six years old and innocent. Children speak whatever comes to their minds. If the palace guards came inquiring, Ramu would innocently say, 'I ate royal brinjals for dinner!'

Tenali smiled and whispered a plan to his wife.

That night, while Ramu was sound asleep on his woven cot, Tenali gently carried the sleeping boy up to the flat rooftop. Clouds drifted across the dark sky, and a gentle night breeze blew. Tenali splashed water droplets over the roof tiles, scooped handfuls of water from a copper jug and let them trickle over the boy's face and arms, while shaking a thin sheet of metal to make low, rumbling sounds: *Rumble, rumble, whoosh! Splash!*

'Wake up, Ramu!' shouted Tenali playfully. 'A wild thunderstorm has broken out! Look at the heavy rain and lightning on the roof!'

The sleepy boy blinked in the darkness, feeling cold water on his brow and hearing the rumbling metal. Tenali then carried him down into the dry bedroom, tucked him under a warm quilt, and let him drift back into peaceful sleep.

The next morning, the head palace gardener discovered two brinjals missing and reported the theft to King Krishna Deva Raya. The King was furious: 'Who dared trespass in my garden? Search every minister's house!'

Soon, royal guards knocked on Tenali Rama's door. 'Tenali, did your household eat royal brinjals last night?'

'Certainly not!' declared Tenali. 'Search our kitchen.' The guards found only rice and lentil soup.

Then the guard chief saw little Ramu playing in the courtyard with clay marbles. 'Come here, little one,' asked the chief kindly. 'What did you have for dinner last night?'

Ramu smiled brightly: 'I ate the most delicious royal brinjal curry with hot rice!'

The guard turned triumphantly to Tenali: 'Aha! The innocent child has spoken the truth! Arrest Tenali Rama!'

Tenali calmly shook his head. 'Wait, officer. Ask the boy what else happened last night before making an arrest.'

The guard turned back to Ramu: 'Tell us what happened after dinner, little boy.'

Ramu's eyes went wide with wonder: 'After dinner, my father and I went up to the rooftop in the middle of the night, and there was a huge thunderstorm! Gallons of rain poured over my head, thunder rumbled across the sky, and lightning flashed across the roof tiles!'

The guard chief blinked in utter disbelief. He looked at the sky and out at the sunny village square. 'Thunderstorm? Heavy rain last night? The skies were crystal clear, with not a single cloud in all of Vijayanagara!'

The guards burst out laughing. 'The poor child is confusing his dreams with reality! He had a vivid dream of eating royal brinjals while dreaming of a rooftop storm!'

The guards apologized and left without making an arrest. When King Krishna Deva Raya heard the guard's report, he saw through the trick, smiled at Tenali's psychological genius, and gifted Tenali a whole basket of royal brinjals with a playful warning never to climb the garden wall again.

One evening, the swan flew to their cottage porch. Sujata and the girls looked in wonder as the radiant bird spoke in a gentle, melodic voice: 'Good mother, do not weep over your poverty. Once every week, I shall visit your porch and shed a single golden feather from my wing. You may sell the feather in the town market, and the gold will provide ample food, warm clothes, and schoolbooks for your children.'

With a gentle flap of his wings, the swan shed one gleaming feather of pure solid gold upon the wooden threshold, then flew back to his lake.

Sujata sold the feather the next morning. The jeweler paid her a handsome sum. For the first time in years, the family had fresh milk, warm blankets, and nutritious vegetables. True to his word, the golden swan returned every seven days, gifting a single golden feather each time. The family's debt vanished, their home was repaired, and the daughters flourished in their studies.

However, as the months passed, a dark, creeping greed began to take root in Sujata's heart. She looked at the cozy home and thought: *'What if the swan flies away across the mountains one day and never returns? Why should we wait week after week for a single feather? If I pluck all his feathers at once, we shall be wealthy for ten generations!'*

Her elder daughter protested with tears in her eyes: 'Mother! The swan is our kindest benefactor! He gives freely from his heart. To harm him or take by force would be cruel and ungrateful!'

Sujata dismissed her daughter's wise plea. The following week, when the golden swan landed gently on the porch, Sujata greeted him with honeyed words. As the unsuspecting swan bowed his neck to shed his feather, Sujata seized him firmly by both wings!

The terrified swan struggled, but Sujata ruthlessly plucked every single feather from his wings and body. Sujata gasped in horror, dropping the coarse white feathers upon the floor. The naked, shivering swan rested on the porch, his eyes filled with profound sorrow, not anger.

The daughters wept and gently carried the shivering bird to a soft nest of dry straw, feeding him grain and nursing his wounds with medicinal oils. Over many weeks, the swan's feathers grew back—not as brilliant gold, but as pure, soft, ordinary white feathers.

As soon as his wings were fully healed, the swan spread his white plumage and took flight into the endless blue sky, never to visit that porch again. Sujata lived the rest of her days in deep remorse, having learned that greed destroys the very blessings that patience and gratitude preserve.

'Do not weep,' replied the frog kindly. 'I can dive down and retrieve your golden treasure. But what will you give me if I bring it back?'

'Whatever you ask, dear frog!' cried the princess eagerly. 'My silk dresses, my pearl necklaces, even the golden crown upon my head!'

The frog shook his head gently: 'I have no need for your dresses, pearls, or golden crowns. But if you will love me, let me be your companion and playmate, let me sit at your table, eat from your golden plate, and sleep in your cozy bed—if you promise me this, I will dive down and bring you the ball.'

'Yes, yes, I promise you everything you wish!' cried the princess. But in her secret heart, she thought: *'What nonsense that silly frog talks! He belongs in the pond with his fellow croakers; how could he ever be a companion to a human princess?'*

Trusting her word, the frog dipped his head beneath the water, swam down into the murky depths, and a moment later surfaced with the gleaming golden ball in his mouth. He tossed it onto the soft moss.

The princess shrieked with joy! She snatched up the golden ball and sprinted back toward the castle as fast as her slippers could carry her.

'Wait! Wait!' croaked the frog from the water. 'Take me with you! I cannot run as fast as you!' But the princess did not turn around; she rushed inside the castle gates and forgot the poor creature completely.

The next evening, as the royal family sat at the grand marble dinner table, a wet, pattering sound came up the marble staircase: *Plip, plop, plip, plop!* Then came a gentle knock at the heavy carved door: 'Youngest princess, open the door for me!'

The princess ran to open the door, but when she saw the green frog sitting on the doormat, she slammed the door shut and hurried back to her chair, pale and trembling.

The King noticed her distress. 'My child, what has frightened you so? Is there a giant outside?'

'No, father,' she confessed in embarrassment. 'It is only a slimy green frog.' She explained how she had dropped her golden ball into the spring and made a promise to the creature, never expecting he could ever leave his pond.

Just then, the knock sounded again: *'Youngest daughter of the King, remember the word you gave by the spring!'*

The wise King looked at his daughter with firm, loving eyes: 'My daughter, that which you have promised in your hour of need, you must faithfully perform. Go at once, open the door, and invite him in.'

The princess bowed her head in shame. She opened the door, and the frog hopped inside, following her to her chair. He ate politely from her plate, and though the princess was hesitant at first, she noticed how gentle, considerate, and well-spoken the frog was.

In the forest, the old gray traveler appeared and said: 'Kind boy, give me a morsel to eat and a drop to drink; I am hungry and thirsty.'

Dummling smiled with open warmth: 'I have only dry ash-bread and sour water, but if that pleases you, sit down with me on this fallen log and let us share it with glad hearts.'

title: [Draft ML] The Little Fir Tree in the Pine Woods

When village children wandered through the woods with baskets filled with wild strawberries, they would sit near the little tree and say: 'Look at this darling little fir! The little tree hated being called 'little.' It sulked and thought: *'Oh, if only I were a tall, majestic tree like the others! Then I could spread my branches wide across the sky, look out over the wide world, and have eagles build their nests in my highest boughs!'*

In the winter, when the snow lay white and glittering like diamonds upon the forest floor, a swift hare would often come leaping past and jump right over the little tree. Oh, how that annoyed him! *'To be so tiny that even a rabbit can hop over my head!'* he fumed.

'Rejoice in your youth!' sang the warm sunbeams. 'Rejoice in your fresh new needles and the sweet sap flowing through your branches!'

And the whispering wind kissed the little tree, and the morning dew wept sparkling tears upon it, but the fir tree understood neither the breeze nor the dew. It wanted only to be tall, to be somewhere else, to become something grander in the future.

Two winters passed, and the little fir had grown so tall that the hare had to run around it. Yet still the tree sighed: *'Growing is not enough! I want to be chopped down and made into the tall mast of a magnificent sailing ship that travels across stormy oceans!'*

When autumn came, woodcutters arrived in the forest. They felled some of the tallest, oldest pine trees with heavy thuds. The little fir tree trembled with mixed fear and longing. A swallow told him that ships across the sea had tall wooden masts that looked splendid and smelled like pine resin.

Then came Christmas Eve. Woodcutters walked through the groves and selected the little fir tree itself, cutting its trunk cleanly. It was carried into a grand mansion, placed in a brass tub filled with sand, and decorated with silk ribbons, gilded apples, walnuts wrapped in silver foil, and dozens of glowing wax candles! At the very top, a golden star sparkled.

That evening, children danced around the tree in pure enchantment. The candles flickered, and the children laughed and sang songs. The fir tree felt proud: *'Now my true glory has arrived!'*

Yet when morning came, the candles were put out. Attendants dismantled the toys and carried the dry tree up into a dark attic corner. The little tree stood alone in the shadows, listening to the dust settle.

In the quiet dark of the attic, the little fir tree finally began to think deeply with an open heart. It remembered the warm sunbeams of the forest. It remembered the gentle mountain breezes. It remembered the songbirds that had sung in its branches and the playful hare leaping over the snow.

*'How beautiful was the forest!'* whispered the tree with a tender sigh of gratitude. *'How sweet was the morning dew! If only I had rejoiced in the glorious sunshine while I had it, instead of constantly wishing my days away!'*

title: [Draft ML] The Cooking Pot That Gave Birth and Passed Away
summary: [Draft ML] When a greedy neighbor lends Mulla Nasruddin a copper cooking pot, Nasruddin returns it with a tiny pot claiming it gave birth. When the neighbor happily accepts, Nasruddin prepares the ultimate lesson in poetic justice.
full_text:
[Draft ML] Mulla Nasruddin had a neighbor named Kasim who was notoriously greedy, selfish, and cunning. Kasim was always eager to take from others, but would never lend a single grain of wheat without demanding interest.

One evening, Nasruddin knocked on Kasim's door. 'Good neighbor Kasim,' said Nasruddin with a humble bow, 'I am preparing a large feast for traveling scholars tonight. Could you please lend me your large copper cooking cauldron for just one day? I shall return it safely tomorrow.'

Kasim hesitated, but seeing a chance to place Nasruddin in his debt, he brought out his heavy copper pot. 'Take it, Mulla. But return it tomorrow without a scratch!'

The next morning, Nasruddin brought the copper cauldron back to Kasim's house. Inside the large pot was a brand-new, tiny copper saucepan.

Kasim inspected the pot and saw the little saucepan. 'Mulla, what is this tiny saucepan doing inside my cauldron?'

Nasruddin beamed with joyful congratulations: 'Rejoice, neighbor Kasim! Last night, while resting in my kitchen, your large cooking pot gave birth to this adorable baby pot! Since the mother pot belongs to you, the baby pot naturally belongs to you as well!'

Kasim stared at Nasruddin. He knew that copper pots do not give birth—that was scientifically impossible! But his insatiable greed whispered: *'Why argue? I am getting a free copper saucepan for nothing!'*

So Kasim smiled broadly and patted Nasruddin on the shoulder: 'How wonderful! Thank you, wise Mulla! Your honesty is commendable!' Kasim gleefully took both pots inside his kitchen.

Two weeks later, Nasruddin visited Kasim again: 'Dear neighbor Kasim, I have another feast tonight. Could you please lend me your large copper cauldron once more?'

Kasim was ecstatic: *'Perhaps it will give birth to twins this time!'* He brought out his finest, heaviest copper cauldron with both hands and handed it to Nasruddin with an eager grin.

One day passed. Then two days. Then a whole week went by, but Nasruddin did not return the pot.

Unable to contain his impatience, Kasim marched over to Nasruddin's house and pounded on the wooden door: 'Nasruddin! Where is my cauldron? Why have you not brought it back?'

Nasruddin opened the door slowly. His eyes were downcast, his shoulders slumped, and he wiped away an imaginary tear with the sleeve of his tunic.

'Alas, my dear brother Kasim!' sighed Nasruddin mournfully. 'I bring you tragic and sorrowful news. Yesterday afternoon, with no warning whatsoever... your beloved copper cauldron passed away! It is dead!'

Kasim turned purple with rage. 'Dead? Are you out of your mind, Nasruddin? How can a copper cooking pot die? Pots are made of metal; they do not have lungs, blood, or life! You are lying to steal my cauldron!'

Mulla Nasruddin looked calmly into Kasim's raging eyes with an amused, serene smile:

'My dear neighbor Kasim, you were perfectly willing to believe that a copper pot could be alive when it gave birth to a baby saucepan for your profit. Why is it so difficult for you to believe that a pot can die when the loss falls upon you? Whatever has the power to be born must surely have the nature to pass away!'

Kasim stood frozen on the doorstep, utterly speechless. His own foolish greed had trapped him completely. The surrounding neighbors who had gathered to listen burst into uncontrollable laughter at Kasim's humiliation. Kasim slunk back into his house in shame, cured forever of taking advantage of others through greedy loopholes.
moral: [Draft ML] You cannot accept an absurd claim when it profits you, and then reject it when it costs you. Greed blinds people to truth and exposes them to poetic justice.

Rashin Coatie tapped the calf's horn. In a twinkle of heather magic, the rough bundle of wool was spun into fine spools of yarn, and before her lay a gown woven of forest-green velvet with gold thistles and a pair of delicate green satin slippers!

Rashin Coatie attended the Yuletide dance. She danced with such natural joy, modesty, and grace that the young Prince was captivated by her kindness. She laughed with the elderly grandmothers, shared cakes with the children, and danced the reel like a mountain breeze.

'Birbal, come to the royal court immediately! But heed my strict conditions: you must arrive at the palace neither walking upon your feet nor riding upon an animal, and you must travel neither under the burning sun nor in the cool shade! If you fail to meet all conditions, you must treat the entire court to a feast!'

The courtiers snickered. 'How can anyone travel without walking or riding? And how can anyone be outside in daylight without being either in the sun or in the shade? Birbal is finally trapped!'

Birbal had taken a lightweight wooden woven cot (a charpai) made with a loose, open mesh of jute rope. He sat comfortably upon the cot, while four strong helpers carried the cot suspended high above their heads, with Birbal resting upon it, so that his own feet never touched the earth, nor was he riding any horse or camel!

Furthermore, because the jute ropes of the cot were woven in an open criss-cross pattern, tiny shafts of sunlight fell through the mesh onto his shoulders while the ropes cast thin criss-cross shadows: he was in alternating lines of sunlight and shadow every inch of the way—neither entirely under the blazing sun nor entirely in the shade!

Birbal arrived before Emperor Akbar's throne, greeted the Emperor with a courteous bow from his floating cot, and smiled cheerfully:

'Your Imperial Majesty, I have arrived as commanded! My feet have not walked a single step, nor did I mount any stallion or beast. And as you can see, the woven ropes keep me partly in the sun and partly in the shade, neither wholly one nor the other!'

Akbar looked at Birbal sitting serenely atop the woven cot, looked at the woven shadows on his shoulders, and burst into uncontrollable laughter. 'Only Birbal could find a third path when given an impossible choice!' Akbar declared, presenting him with a purse of gold and ordering cool sherbet for his loyal helpers.

As the old man drew closer, Akbar noticed from his cloudy, unblinking eyes that the man was completely sightless.

title: [Draft ML] The Three Golden Statues and the Wire Test

[Draft ML] A grand envoy from an overseas empire arrived at the royal court of Vijayanagara, presenting three magnificent statues crafted from solid, gleaming gold. The three statues appeared completely identical in height, weight, polish, and facial expression. Each depicted a graceful human figure with hands resting quietly at its side.

The envoy presented the challenge to King Krishna Deva Raya: 'Sire, though these three golden statues appear identical to the eye and touch, one of them is of low value, the second is of middling value, and the third is of supreme, peerless value! If your scholars can determine which is which, and explain the reason why, our ruler will enter into a permanent alliance of honor with your kingdom.'

All the court jewelers, sculptors, and mathematicians stepped forward. They weighed the statues on brass balances—every statue weighed exactly fifty pounds. They measured the height—every statue stood exactly three feet tall. They tested the gold purity—every statue was made of flawless twenty-four karat gold. The courtiers were utterly confounded.

King Krishna Deva Raya turned to his trusted wit: 'Tenali, our royal honor rests upon your shoulders. Can you discern the difference between these three identical figures?'

'Give me a slender, flexible piece of silver wire, Your Majesty,' Tenali Rama smiled.

An attendant brought a spool of fine silver wire. Tenali walked to the first statue. Inspecting the ears carefully, he noticed a tiny, hairline hole in the ear canal. Tenali gently fed the flexible wire into the first statue's ear. The wire pushed through, and a moment later, the tip of the wire slipped out of the statue's **mouth**!

Tenali walked to the second statue and fed the wire into its ear. The wire curled inside the head, traveled downward through the neck, and emerged out through the statue's **other ear**!

Finally, Tenali fed the wire into the ear of the third statue. The wire traveled inward and disappeared deep into the statue's **heart**, with no wire coming out of the mouth, other ear, or any other opening at all!

Tenali turned to the King and the foreign envoy with a beaming smile:

'Your Majesty, the mystery is solved!' Tenali announced. 'The first statue represents the person of lowest value: whatever words or secrets enter their ear immediately spill out of their mouth in careless gossip! They cannot be trusted with any confidential trust.'

'The second statue represents the person of middling value: whatever words enter one ear go straight out the other ear without leaving any impression! They listen without understanding or caring, forgetting everything they are told.'

'And the third statue,' Tenali concluded with reverent dignity, 'represents the person of supreme, priceless value: whatever is spoken to their ear travels straight to their heart! They absorb wisdom, keep confidences sacred, and cherish their friends with unwavering loyalty.'

The foreign envoy fell to his knees in profound admiration. 'Incredible, wise Tenali! That is the exact philosophical riddle intended by our king!'

King Krishna Deva Raya rewarded Tenali with a necklace of emeralds, reminding everyone that a person's true worth is determined by how faithfully they listen and protect what is shared in confidence.
moral: [Draft ML] Listen with your heart. Avoid careless gossip and inattentive ears; be the person who holds secrets sacred and treasures wisdom deep within.

[Draft ML] On a brilliant, starry night, Mulla Nasruddin went out to his garden well to draw a bucket of cool water before bedtime. The sky was a vast canopy of indigo, and the full moon shone like a polished silver plate.

Nasruddin leaned over the stone rim of the well and peered into the water below. To his utter shock and dismay, right there in the dark circular depths of the well, floating peacefully on the surface of the water, was the bright, round moon!

Nasruddin gasped in horror, clutching his turban with both hands: 'Great heavens! The poor moon has lost its footing in the heavens and fallen straight into my well! If I do not rescue the moon immediately, the entire world will be plunged into eternal night, travelers will lose their way in the desert, and children will have no moonbeams to sing them to sleep!'

Filled with heroic urgency, Nasruddin sprinted to his tool shed. He found a sturdy hemp rope and tied a heavy three-pronged iron grappling hook to one end. Hurrying back to the well, he tossed the hook down into the darkness.

'Do not panic, dear Moon!' called Nasruddin down the well. 'Hold on tight! Nasruddin is here to pull you back to the sky!'

Nasruddin lowered the hook into the water. He swirled the rope around until—*Clink! Clank!*—the iron hook caught firmly beneath a heavy, jagged stone ledge deep within the well wall. The rope went completely taut.

Nasruddin beamed with triumph: *'Aha! I have caught the moon by its horns!'*

He planted his worn sandals firmly against the mossy stone rim, gripped the coarse rope with both hands, leaned backward with all his weight, and pulled with heroic, grunting effort: *'Heave... ho! Heave... ho!'*

The rope did not budge. The stone was wedged tight. Nasruddin strained harder and harder. His face turned red as a pomegranate, his eyes bulged, and his veins stood out on his forehead. With one final, titanic, superhuman pull—*SNAP!*—the rope snapped cleanly in half!

Sent flying backward by the sudden release of tension, Nasruddin tumbled through the air, flipped over, and landed flat on his back in the soft clover with a loud: *OOMPH!*

For a moment, Nasruddin lay in the grass, bruised and seeing twinkling stars. As his breath returned, he slowly opened his eyes and looked straight up into the boundless sky above.

There, floating gracefully above the pine trees, riding peacefully among the silver clouds, was the glorious, brilliant full moon, shining down upon his garden in all its majestic glory!

Nasruddin let out a long, happy sigh of deep contentment. He dusted off his trousers, smiled with peaceful pride, and whispered:

'Well, well! I may have bruised my back and torn my tunic, but by heaven, what a splendid success! I pulled so hard that I launched the moon right out of the well and threw it all the way back up into the highest sky!'

Chuckling with joyful satisfaction, the wise Mulla went inside his cottage, drank a glass of water, and slept the deep, peaceful sleep of someone who believed with all his heart that he had saved the night sky for the world.
